cable_kickback.summary: A one-arm triceps extension done bent over at a low cable, finishing with the arm straight back. The cable keeps tension on the triceps at full lockout, where a dumbbell kickback goes slack. Good as a light finisher for anyone chasing triceps size.
cable_kickback.musclesNote: The triceps straighten the elbow against the cable; all three heads work, and keeping the upper arm slightly behind the torso puts more stretch on the long head. The rear delt and lats only hold the upper arm still.
setup: Set a single handle or no handle (grab the cable ball) at the lowest pulley, or about knee height.
Step back, hinge forward until your torso is about 45 degrees or flatter, and brace with your free hand on your thigh.
Pin your working upper arm against your side, parallel to the floor or slightly above.
Start with the elbow bent about 90 degrees and the hand under the elbow.
execution: Straighten the elbow until the arm is fully locked out behind you.
Hold the lockout for a one-second squeeze without letting the upper arm drop.
Lower under control for 2 seconds back to about 90 degrees of elbow bend.
Keep the shoulder still; only the forearm should move.

mistakes.fix: Lock the upper arm to your side and lighten the weight until only the elbow moves.
Pick a load you can fully straighten and squeeze for a second on every rep.
Hinge further so the cable pulls against the forearm through the whole range.

cable_kickback.progression: Kickbacks progress best by reps: work up to 15-20 clean reps, then take the smallest stack increment. If the stack jumps are too big, add a pause at lockout instead.

faq.q: Are cable kickbacks better than dumbbell kickbacks?
faq.a: For most people, yes. The cable keeps tension at lockout and through the start of the rep, while the dumbbell only loads the top. Use whichever you can do with a still upper arm.

faq.q: Are kickbacks a good triceps builder?
faq.a: They are a useful accessory, not a main builder, because the load stays light. Pair them with a heavier press or extension like close grip bench or overhead extensions.

cable_overhead_extension.summary: A triceps extension done facing away from a cable with the arms overhead, usually with a rope. Working from a full stretch makes it one of the best isolation lifts for the long head. Suits anyone who can get their arms overhead comfortably.
cable_overhead_extension.musclesNote: The triceps extend the elbow; with the arms overhead, the long head (which crosses the shoulder) is stretched hardest, so this targets it better than pushdowns. The core keeps the ribs down while you press.
setup: Attach a rope to a pulley set around hip to chest height.
Grab the rope, turn away from the stack, and step forward into a staggered stance.
Lean slightly forward with elbows pointing ahead and hands behind your head.
Brace your abs so your lower back does not arch.
execution: Extend the elbows until the arms are straight in front of and above your head.
Spread the rope ends slightly at the finish.
Lower for 2-3 seconds until your hands are behind your head and you feel a deep stretch.
Keep the elbows roughly in place; let the forearms do the moving.

mistakes.fix: Keep the elbows about shoulder width and pointed forward throughout.
Let the hands travel all the way behind the head under control; the stretch is the point.
Use a staggered stance, brace your abs, and lean the torso slightly forward.

cable_overhead_extension.progression: Build to 12-15 controlled reps with a full stretch before adding a plate. If setup gets awkward at heavy loads, switch to a single-arm version or a seated overhead dumbbell extension.

faq.q: Is the cable overhead extension good for the long head?
faq.a: Yes. Because the arms are overhead, the long head is lengthened, and training it in that stretched position is a strong stimulus for growth.

faq.q: Rope or straight bar for overhead extensions?
faq.a: The rope lets the wrists rotate and the hands separate, which is easier on the elbows for most people. A straight bar works if the rope feels unstable.

preacher_curl.summary: A biceps curl done with the upper arms resting on an angled pad, usually with an EZ bar. The pad stops any swinging and makes the bottom of the curl the hardest part. Good for anyone who cheats on standing curls or wants strict biceps work.
preacher_curl.musclesNote: The biceps flex the elbow, with the brachialis and brachioradialis helping. The pad fixes the upper arm in front of the body, which shortens the biceps at the shoulder and puts the hardest loading near the bottom of the rep.
setup: Set the seat so your armpits sit snugly at the top of the pad.
Rest the back of your upper arms flat on the pad.
Take a shoulder-width underhand grip on the angled parts of the EZ bar.
Start with the arms nearly straight but not hyperextended.
execution: Curl the bar up until your forearms are close to vertical.
Stop before the bar comes so close that tension drops off.
Lower slowly for 2-3 seconds to a near-straight arm.
Keep the upper arms and shoulders pinned to the pad the whole time.

mistakes.mistake: Dropping the bar at the bottom
mistakes.fix: Control the last few inches; the bottom is where the biceps are most loaded and most vulnerable.

mistakes.mistake: Lifting the elbows off the pad
mistakes.fix: Keep the back of the arms flat on the pad and reduce the weight if they rise.
Sit tall, keep the chest up, and let only the forearms move.

preacher_curl.progression: Add reps until you hit about 12, then go up the smallest step, usually 5 lb total. Preacher curls do not tolerate big jumps; if form breaks, back off rather than bouncing out of the bottom.

faq.q: Are preacher curls better than barbell curls?
faq.a: Neither is better; they load the curl differently. Preacher curls are stricter and hardest near the bottom, while standing curls allow more weight. Many people use both.

faq.q: Why do preacher curls hurt my elbows?
faq.a: Usually the load is too heavy or the bottom is dropped too fast. Use lighter weight, slow down the last part of the descent, and stop just short of locking the elbow.

incline_dumbbell_curl.summary: A dumbbell curl done lying back on an incline bench so the arms hang behind the body. This places the biceps on a long stretch at the start of each rep. A strong choice for lifters who want biceps size and already handle basic curls well.
incline_dumbbell_curl.musclesNote: The biceps flex the elbow and supinate the forearm; the arms hanging behind the torso stretch the long head across the shoulder. Brachialis and forearm muscles assist.
setup: Set an adjustable bench to about 45-60 degrees.
Sit back with your head and upper back on the pad.
Let the dumbbells hang straight down at your sides, palms forward.
Keep your shoulders back against the bench, not rolled forward.
execution: Curl both dumbbells (or alternate) without letting your elbows drift forward much.
Squeeze at the top with palms facing up.
Lower for 2-3 seconds all the way to a straight, hanging arm.
Pause briefly at the bottom to feel the stretch before the next rep.

mistakes.fix: Keep the upper arms close to vertical so the biceps do the work, not the front delts.
If your shoulders feel strained, raise the bench angle until the stretch is strong but comfortable.

mistakes.mistake: Lifting the head and shoulders off the pad
mistakes.fix: Keep your back on the bench and use lighter dumbbells.

incline_dumbbell_curl.progression: Expect to use noticeably lighter weight than standing curls. Push reps to 12-15 before moving up a dumbbell size, and keep the full stretch at the bottom.

faq.q: Why are incline curls harder than regular curls?
faq.a: The arms start behind the body, so the biceps work from a longer, weaker position and you cannot use momentum. That is the reason to do them.

faq.q: Are incline dumbbell curls safe for the shoulder?
faq.a: For most people, yes, when the load is moderate. If the front of the shoulder feels strained, raise the bench angle and reduce the weight.

concentration_curl.summary: A seated, one-arm dumbbell curl with the elbow braced against the inner thigh. It removes body swing entirely, so it is a strict way to feel the biceps work. Useful as a finisher or for lifters learning to control a curl.
concentration_curl.musclesNote: The biceps flex the elbow and supinate the forearm, with the brachialis helping. Bracing the arm against the thigh keeps the shoulder out of it, so the biceps handle almost all the work.
setup: Sit on the end of a bench with your feet wider than shoulder width.
Hold a dumbbell in one hand and lean forward slightly.
Rest the back of your upper arm against the inside of the same-side thigh.
Let the arm hang nearly straight, palm facing away from the leg.
execution: Curl the dumbbell toward your shoulder, keeping the upper arm on the thigh.
Squeeze at the top for a second with the pinky slightly turned up.
Lower for 2-3 seconds to a nearly straight arm.
Finish all reps on one side, then switch.

mistakes.mistake: Using the thigh to push the arm
mistakes.fix: Rest the arm on the thigh but do not drive it with the leg.
Lower until the arm is nearly straight each rep.
Keep the torso still and drop the weight if you need to lean back to finish.

concentration_curl.progression: Use reps first: build to 12-15 per arm, then move up the smallest dumbbell jump. Because it is strict and unilateral, it is better as a second or third curl than your main heavy one.

faq.q: Do concentration curls build the biceps peak?
faq.a: No exercise can change the shape of your biceps; that is genetic. Concentration curls do build the biceps as a whole, which makes them look fuller.

faq.q: Are concentration curls better than hammer curls?
faq.a: They train different emphases. Concentration curls target the biceps with a supinated grip, while hammer curls shift more work to the brachialis and brachioradialis.

machine_row.summary: A seated, plate-loaded row with a chest pad and independent or linked handles. The chest pad takes the lower back out of the lift, so you can load the upper back hard without fatigue limiting you elsewhere. Suits beginners and experienced lifters alike.
machine_row.musclesNote: The lats, rhomboids, and mid traps pull the arms back and squeeze the shoulder blades together; the rear delts and biceps assist. Lower, closer handles bias the lats; wider, higher handles shift work to the upper back.
setup: Adjust the seat so the handles line up around lower chest height when your arms are straight.
Set your chest firmly against the pad.
Choose a grip: neutral or narrow for lats, wide or overhand for upper back.
Start with arms fully extended and shoulders allowed to reach forward.
execution: Pull the handles back by driving your elbows toward your hips or ribs.
Squeeze the shoulder blades together for a moment at the end.
Return for 2 seconds until the arms are straight and the shoulder blades spread.
Keep your chest on the pad the whole time.

mistakes.fix: Keep the chest pressed into the pad and reduce weight if you have to lean back to finish.
Let the arms fully straighten and the shoulder blades reach forward each rep.
Think of pulling the elbows back and down, not the shoulders up to the ears.

machine_row.progression: Add reps in the 8-12 range, then add a 10 lb plate per side or a smaller plate if available. Machines are a good place to push close to failure safely.

faq.q: Is a machine row as good as a barbell row?
faq.a: For building the back, it can be just as good, and often better for high effort because your lower back is supported. Barbell rows add more trunk and hip demand.

faq.q: Should I use one arm at a time on a row machine?
faq.a: If the handles move independently, single-arm work helps fix side-to-side imbalances and allows a slightly bigger range. Both ways work.

t_bar_row.summary: A bent-over row using a bar anchored at one end (a landmine or a dedicated T-bar station) with a V-handle or grips near the loaded end. It lets you row heavy with a neutral grip and a fixed path. Good for intermediate lifters wanting a heavy back builder.
t_bar_row.musclesNote: The lats, rhomboids, and traps pull the weight up and squeeze the shoulder blades back, with the biceps and rear delts assisting. The hamstrings, glutes, and lower back work isometrically to hold the hinge.
setup: Straddle the bar near the plates and attach a V-handle under the bar, or use the station's grips.
Hinge at the hips with soft knees until your torso is about 30-45 degrees above parallel.
Brace your trunk and keep a flat back.
Let the weight hang at arm's length, shoulders reaching down.
execution: Row the handle toward your lower chest or upper stomach.
Drive the elbows back past the torso and squeeze the upper back.
Lower for 2 seconds until the arms are straight.
Keep the torso angle steady; do not stand up to finish the rep.

mistakes.fix: Hold your torso angle and use a weight you can row without rising.
Brace before each rep and stop the set when you can no longer hold a flat back.

mistakes.mistake: Using big plates that cut the range
mistakes.fix: Use smaller-diameter plates (like 25s) so the plates do not hit your chest before full range.

t_bar_row.progression: Add a small plate once you hit the top of your rep range, usually 8-12. If your lower back tires before your upper back, switch to a chest-supported T-bar or machine row.

faq.q: Is the T-bar row good for back thickness?
faq.a: Yes. It lets you row heavy with a fixed path, which loads the mid back, lats, and traps well.

faq.q: T-bar row vs barbell row?
faq.a: The T-bar's arc and neutral grip are often easier on the wrists and lower back, and it is easier to keep a steady torso. Barbell rows allow more grip options. Both build the back.

chest_supported_row.summary: A dumbbell row done lying face down on an incline bench. The bench supports the torso, so you can train the upper back hard without your lower back or momentum getting involved. Ideal for anyone with a cranky lower back or who tends to cheat rows.
chest_supported_row.musclesNote: The lats, rhomboids, and mid traps row the dumbbells and pull the shoulder blades together, with biceps and rear delts assisting. Elbows tucked biases the lats; elbows flared at about 45-70 degrees shifts work to the upper back and rear delts.
setup: Set an adjustable bench to about 30-45 degrees.
Lie face down with your chest on the pad and your chin just over the top.
Plant your feet or toes on the floor for stability.
Hold the dumbbells hanging straight down, shoulders reaching toward the floor.
execution: Row the dumbbells up by driving the elbows back.
Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the top for a moment.
Lower for 2 seconds to a full stretch with the arms straight.
Keep your chest on the pad; do not lift it to finish reps.

mistakes.mistake: Lifting the chest off the bench
mistakes.fix: Keep the sternum on the pad and lighten the load if you need body English.

mistakes.mistake: Bench too flat or too steep
mistakes.fix: Find an angle where the dumbbells hang clear of the floor and you can still breathe comfortably.
Let the shoulder blades spread fully at the bottom of each rep.

chest_supported_row.progression: Progress reps in the 8-15 range, then move up one dumbbell size. If your gym's dumbbells jump in big increments, add reps or a pause at the top before moving up.

faq.q: Are chest supported rows good for the lower back?
faq.a: They are useful because the bench supports your torso, so your lower back does very little. That makes them a good row option when the back is tired or sore.

faq.q: Chest supported row vs bent over row?
faq.a: The chest supported row isolates the upper back better and limits cheating. The bent over row trains the hinge and trunk too, but fatigue there can limit how hard the back works.

meadows_row.summary: A single-arm row standing beside a landmine-anchored barbell, gripping the end of the sleeve overhand. It gives a big stretch and lets you load one side heavily. Best for intermediate lifters looking to build lats and upper back.
meadows_row.musclesNote: The lats, rhomboids, and traps do the pulling, with the rear delts and biceps assisting. The overhand grip on the thick sleeve also works the forearms, and the staggered stance asks the hips and trunk to resist rotation.
setup: Anchor one end of a barbell in a landmine or corner and load the other end.
Stand perpendicular to the bar, front foot near the plates and back leg staggered behind.
Hinge until your torso is close to parallel and rest your non-working forearm on your front knee.
Grip the end of the sleeve overhand with the working hand.
execution: Row the bar up and back, driving the elbow up and slightly out.
Pull until the elbow passes the torso; stop before the plates touch your arm.
Lower slowly to a full stretch, letting the shoulder blade move forward.
Keep the hips square; avoid twisting to lift the weight.

mistakes.fix: Brace on the front knee and keep the hips and shoulders square to the floor.
Use 25 lb or smaller plates to get a fuller range without them hitting you.
Use straps if your grip fails before your back.

meadows_row.progression: Progress in small plates (2.5-10 lb) once you hit 8-12 clean reps per side. If grip limits you, add straps rather than shortening the range.

faq.q: What does the Meadows row work?
faq.a: Mainly the lats and upper back, with biceps, rear delts, and forearms helping. The single-arm setup also challenges trunk stability.

faq.q: Can I do a Meadows row without a landmine?
faq.a: Yes. Wedge the empty end of the barbell into a corner, ideally wrapped in a towel, so it cannot slide or damage the wall.

landmine_press.summary: A press using a barbell anchored at one end, pushing the loaded end up and forward. The angled path suits many shoulders better than a strict overhead press. Suits beginners, lifters with limited overhead mobility, and athletes.
landmine_press.musclesNote: The front delts and upper chest press the bar up and forward, the triceps straighten the elbow, and the serratus helps the shoulder blade rotate. Done one-arm or half-kneeling, the abs and obliques also resist twisting.
setup: Anchor a barbell in a landmine or corner and load the free end.
Stand (or half-kneel) facing the bar, holding the end of the sleeve at shoulder height.
Stagger your feet or keep them hip width, and brace your trunk.
Keep the elbow slightly in front of the body, not flared out wide.
execution: Press the bar up and forward until your arm is straight.
Let your shoulder blade reach forward at the top.
Lower under control back to the front of the shoulder.
Keep your ribs down; do not lean back to finish.

mistakes.fix: Brace the abs and squeeze the glutes, or switch to half-kneeling to lock the hips.
Keep the elbow tucked at about 30-45 degrees from the body.
Use a staggered stance and a load you can press without rotating.

landmine_press.progression: Add reps in the 8-12 range, then add a small plate. Once standing presses feel easy, a strict dumbbell or barbell overhead press is the natural next step if your shoulders tolerate it.

faq.q: Is the landmine press good for shoulders?
faq.a: Yes. It trains the front delts and upper chest with an angled path that many people find more comfortable than pressing straight overhead.

faq.q: Landmine press vs overhead press?
faq.a: The overhead press trains a full vertical press and allows heavier loads. The landmine press is easier to learn, kinder to stiff shoulders, and works well one arm at a time.

deficit_rdl.summary: A Romanian deadlift done standing on a low platform so the bar can travel lower. The extra range puts the hamstrings and glutes on a longer stretch. Best for lifters who already own a solid RDL and have the hamstring flexibility to use the extra depth.
deficit_rdl.musclesNote: The hamstrings and glutes lengthen as you hinge and then extend the hip to stand. The lower back muscles hold the spine neutral; if you cannot keep a flat back at the bottom, the deficit is too deep.
setup: Stand on a stable 1-3 inch platform or a sturdy plate, feet hip width.
Hold the bar with a double overhand or mixed grip just outside the thighs.
Start standing tall, knees softly bent, lats tight.
Brace your trunk before each rep.
execution: Push the hips straight back and slide the bar down the thighs.
Keep the bar close and the knees at a fixed soft bend.
Lower until you reach your hamstring limit with a flat back, often mid-shin or lower.
Drive the hips forward to stand, squeezing the glutes at the top.

mistakes.mistake: Rounding the back to reach the bottom
mistakes.fix: Only go as low as you can with a neutral spine; the deficit is not a target.
Keep shins near vertical and push the hips back rather than bending the knees more.
Keep the lats engaged and the bar brushing your legs throughout.

deficit_rdl.progression: Use less weight than your standard RDL at first and progress by 5-10 lb jumps once you hit your target reps. If depth is limited by flexibility, keep doing regular RDLs until it improves.

faq.q: Is a deficit RDL better than a regular RDL?
faq.a: Only if you can use the extra range with a flat back. For many lifters, a regular RDL reaches full hamstring stretch already.

faq.q: How high should the deficit be for RDLs?
faq.a: Usually 1-3 inches. Anything higher tends to force rounding for most people.

single_leg_rdl.summary: A one-leg hinge with dumbbells, tipping forward on the standing leg as the free leg reaches back. It trains hamstrings and glutes one side at a time and challenges balance. Good for runners, field-sport athletes, and anyone with side-to-side imbalances.
single_leg_rdl.musclesNote: The standing leg's hamstrings and glutes lengthen and then extend the hip; the glute medius and foot muscles stabilize against tipping. The lower back holds the spine neutral as you hinge.
setup: Hold a dumbbell in the hand opposite the standing leg, or one in each hand.
Stand on one foot with a soft knee.
Brace your trunk and square your hips to the floor.
Use a wall or rack with your free hand for balance if needed.
execution: Hinge forward at the hip while the free leg reaches straight back.
Keep the hips level and the back flat; lower until your hamstring is stretched.
Drive through the standing foot to return upright.
Move slowly enough to control balance throughout.

mistakes.fix: Keep the back toe pointed down and both hip points facing the floor.

mistakes.mistake: Rounding the back to reach lower
mistakes.fix: Lower only until the hamstring stretches with a flat back.
Hold a support with your free hand so you can load the leg properly.

single_leg_rdl.progression: Master bodyweight first, then add dumbbells in small jumps. If balance limits you more than the muscles, use a support or switch to a kickstand (staggered stance) RDL.

faq.q: Single leg RDL vs regular RDL?
faq.a: The regular RDL lets you lift much heavier. The single leg version adds balance and hip stability work and can help even out side-to-side differences.

faq.q: What is the hardest part of single-leg RDLs?
faq.a: For most people it's balance, not strength. Use a light hand support or a kickstand stance so you can push the muscles harder.

good_morning.summary: A barbell hinge with the bar on your upper back, bowing forward at the hips with soft knees. It works the hamstrings, glutes, and spinal erectors and builds hip strength for squats and deadlifts. Best for intermediate lifters with a solid hinge pattern.
good_morning.musclesNote: The hamstrings and glutes lengthen as you hinge and extend the hip to bring you back up. The erector spinae work hard to keep the spine from rounding, more so than in an RDL because the load sits higher.
setup: Set the bar in a rack at upper-chest height and place it across your upper back as for a squat.
Unrack, step back, and stand feet hip to shoulder width with soft knees.
Take a big breath and brace your trunk.
Pull your shoulder blades tight to hold the bar securely.
execution: Push the hips back and lower your torso while keeping a flat back.
Stop when your hamstrings are fully stretched or your torso is near parallel, whichever comes first.
Drive the hips forward to return upright.
Keep the weight in your midfoot; avoid shifting onto the toes.

mistakes.fix: Stop the descent sooner and reduce the weight until you can keep the spine neutral.
Keep the knees soft but mostly fixed so it stays a hinge, not a squat.
Start with an empty bar and add small jumps; this lift is accessory work, not a max lift.

good_morning.progression: Keep good mornings in moderate rep ranges (6-12) and add 5-10 lb at a time. If your back fatigues before your hamstrings, use an RDL instead.

faq.q: Are good mornings safe?
faq.a: They are safe when the load is moderate and your back stays flat. Most problems come from going too heavy or too deep.

faq.q: Good morning vs RDL?
faq.a: Both are hip hinges. The good morning loads the bar higher, which works the lower back harder and uses less weight. The RDL is easier to learn and to load heavy.

front_squat.summary: A barbell squat with the bar held on the front of the shoulders. The front load keeps the torso upright, which makes it very quad-dominant and demanding on the upper back and core. Good for lifters who want strong quads and better squat posture.
front_squat.musclesNote: The quads extend the knee, and the glutes extend the hip. The upper back and abs work hard to keep you upright under the bar; if they give out, the bar rolls forward.
setup: Set the bar in a rack at upper chest height.
Hold the bar in a front rack (fingers under the bar, elbows high) or with arms crossed.
Unrack and step back into a shoulder-width stance, toes turned out slightly.
Raise your elbows and brace before each rep.
execution: Squat down by bending the knees and hips together, keeping the torso upright.
Let the knees travel forward over the toes.
Descend to at least thighs parallel, deeper if you can stay upright.
Drive up with the elbows high and the chest leading.

mistakes.fix: Drive the elbows up as you rise out of the hole.
Use fewer fingers under the bar, loosen the grip, or try straps or a crossed-arm grip.
Sit down between your heels and use squat shoes or small plates under the heels if ankles are stiff.

front_squat.progression: Add 5-10 lb a session as a beginner, then smaller weekly jumps. Expect to use less than your back squat; upper back and rack position usually limit it before the legs do.

faq.q: Front squat vs back squat?
faq.a: The front squat keeps you more upright and is more quad focused. The back squat lets you lift heavier and uses more glute and hip. Both are worth doing.

faq.q: Why is the front squat so hard on the wrists?
faq.a: Usually limited wrist, triceps, or lat flexibility. Holding the bar with fingertips or using straps can help while flexibility improves.

sissy_squat.summary: A bodyweight squat where you lean back and let the knees travel far forward while rising up on the toes. It isolates the quads, especially the rectus femoris, with no equipment. Good as a finisher for intermediate or advanced lifters with healthy knees.
sissy_squat.musclesNote: The quads extend the knee through a long range, with the rectus femoris stretched as the hips stay open. The abs and hip flexors hold the body straight from knees to shoulders.
setup: Stand with feet hip-width apart near a rack or post.
Hold the support with one hand for balance.
Rise onto the balls of your feet.
Keep your hips straight and your torso in line with your thighs.
execution: Push your knees forward and lean back as you lower.
Lower as far as you can control, often until the knees are well past the toes.
Pause briefly at the bottom.
Drive through the balls of your feet and straighten the knees to return.

mistakes.fix: Keep the hips extended and the body in a straight line from knees to shoulders.
Lower for 2-3 seconds and only go as deep as you can control.
Start with a partial range and increase depth over weeks as the knees adapt.

sissy_squat.progression: Start with partial reps and build to full range over several weeks. Then add load by holding a plate to the chest or slowing the descent.

faq.q: Are sissy squats bad for your knees?
faq.a: They place a lot of load on the knees, so they suit people without knee pain. Start with partial range and build up gradually.

faq.q: Do sissy squats build quads?
faq.a: Yes. They isolate the quads through a long range of motion, making them an effective finisher.

reverse_lunge.summary: A lunge where you step backward instead of forward, holding dumbbells at your sides. Stepping back is generally easier on the knees and easier to balance than a forward lunge. Good for beginners and anyone building single-leg strength.
reverse_lunge.musclesNote: The quads and glutes of the front leg do most of the work; a more upright torso biases the quads, a slight forward lean biases the glutes. The adductors and hip stabilizers also work to keep the knee in line.
setup: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding dumbbells at your sides.
Brace your trunk and keep your chest up.
Shift weight to the front leg before stepping.
execution: Step one foot back far enough that both knees can bend to about 90 degrees.
Lower until the back knee nearly touches the floor.
Drive through the front foot's heel and midfoot to return to standing.
Alternate legs or finish all reps on one side.

mistakes.fix: Step back far enough that the front shin stays fairly vertical at the bottom.
Keep the knee tracking over the middle toes.
Keep most weight on the front leg so it does the work.

reverse_lunge.progression: Build to 10-12 reps per leg, then go up one dumbbell size. Once grip limits you, use straps, a barbell, or move to a Bulgarian split squat.

faq.q: Reverse lunge vs forward lunge?
faq.a: The reverse lunge is easier to balance and usually gentler on the knees. The forward lunge adds a braking demand to the quads. Both work the same muscles.

faq.q: Do reverse lunges work glutes or quads?
faq.a: Both. Staying upright shifts work toward the quads, while leaning forward slightly puts more on the glutes.

step_up.summary: A single-leg exercise where you step onto a box or bench holding dumbbells, then step down. It trains the quads and glutes with a balance demand and transfers well to stairs and sport. Good for beginners and athletes.
step_up.musclesNote: The working leg's quads and glutes extend the knee and hip to lift you onto the box. A higher box increases glute and hip demand; a lower box keeps it quad dominant.
setup: Use a stable box or bench around knee height or lower.
Hold dumbbells at your sides.
Place one whole foot flat on the box.
Stand tall with your chest up and your trunk braced.
execution: Drive through the top foot to stand up onto the box.
Keep the back foot passive; avoid pushing off the floor.
Stand fully at the top, then lower slowly back down with control.
Finish all reps on one side before switching.

mistakes.fix: Lift the back toes slightly or keep them light so the top leg does the work.
Choose a height where your hip is no higher than your knee at the start.
Lower for 2 seconds on the way down instead of falling off the box.

step_up.progression: Build to 10-12 reps per leg, then increase dumbbell weight. Raise the box only if you can keep good control.

faq.q: Are step ups good for glutes?
faq.a: Yes, especially with a higher box and a slight forward lean. A lower box puts more emphasis on the quads.

faq.q: How high should the box be for step ups?
faq.a: Usually around knee height or slightly lower. Your thigh should be no higher than parallel at the start.

bodyweight_squat.summary: A squat with no external load, also called an air squat. It teaches the squat pattern, builds basic leg endurance, and works as a warm-up. Good for beginners and anyone without equipment.
bodyweight_squat.musclesNote: The quads extend the knee and the glutes extend the hip. Without load, it is more of a movement and endurance drill than a strength builder for trained lifters.
setup: Stand with feet about shoulder width apart, toes turned out slightly.
Keep your weight across the whole foot.
Hold your arms out in front or clasp your hands at your chest.
Brace your trunk.
execution: Bend the knees and hips together to sit down between your heels.
Keep the chest up and the knees in line with the toes.
Go to at least thighs parallel, deeper if you can keep your heels down.
Stand back up by driving through your feet.

mistakes.fix: Shift weight to midfoot and limit depth until ankle mobility improves.
Push your knees outward in line with your toes.
Keep the chest up and reach the arms forward for balance.

bodyweight_squat.progression: Build to 20-30 controlled reps, then add load with a goblet squat or slow the tempo. Once bodyweight is easy, move to weighted squats.

faq.q: How many bodyweight squats should I do?
faq.a: Start with 2-3 sets of 10-20. Once you can do 30 easily, add weight or harder variations.

faq.q: Can bodyweight squats build muscle?
faq.a: Beginners may see some growth. Most people need added load or harder variations to keep progressing.

nordic_curl.summary: A kneeling bodyweight hamstring exercise where you slowly lower your torso toward the floor with your ankles anchored. It is very demanding on the hamstrings, especially the lowering phase. Good for intermediate and advanced lifters and athletes.
nordic_curl.musclesNote: The hamstrings resist knee extension as you lower, working hard while lengthening. The glutes help keep the hips extended so the body stays in a straight line.
setup: Kneel on a pad with your ankles secured under a bench, partner, or anchor.
Keep your body straight from knees to head.
Cross your arms or hold your hands in front ready to catch yourself.
Squeeze your glutes to keep the hips extended.
execution: Lower your torso forward as slowly as you can, keeping the hips straight.
Catch yourself with your hands when you can no longer control the descent.
Push lightly off the floor and pull with the hamstrings to return.
Aim for a 3-5 second lowering phase.

mistakes.fix: Keep glutes squeezed so you lower as one straight line.
Control the lowering and catch yourself early rather than falling.
Start with low volume, such as 2-3 sets of 3-5, because soreness can be severe.

nordic_curl.progression: Start with lowering-only reps and use your hands to push back up. Progress by controlling more of the range, then adding full reps.

faq.q: Are nordic curls good for hamstrings?
faq.a: Yes. They heavily load the hamstrings during lowering, which builds strength and size.

faq.q: Why are nordic curls so hard?
faq.a: Your bodyweight creates a long lever, and few people can control the full range at first. Use partial range or a band for assistance.

hip_thrust_bw.summary: A floor-based bridge where you lie on your back and lift your hips by driving through your feet. It targets the glutes with no equipment and is easy to learn. Good for beginners, warm-ups, and home training.
hip_thrust_bw.musclesNote: The glutes extend the hip to lift the pelvis, with the hamstrings assisting. Feet closer to the hips shift more work to the glutes; feet further away increase hamstring involvement.
setup: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat, about hip width apart.
Place your feet so your shins are near vertical at the top.
Rest your arms on the floor by your sides.
Tuck your ribs down and brace lightly.
execution: Drive through your heels and lift your hips until your body forms a line from shoulders to knees.
Squeeze your glutes at the top for 1-2 seconds.
Lower slowly until your hips almost touch the floor.
Keep the ribs down; do not arch your lower back to get higher.

mistakes.fix: Keep the ribs down and finish the lift with the glutes, not the back.
Bring the feet closer so the shins are near vertical at the top.
Pause at the top and lower under control.

hip_thrust_bw.progression: Build to 20+ reps, then progress to single-leg glute bridges, a pause at the top, or add weight on the hips. Move to barbell hip thrusts when bodyweight is easy.

faq.q: Glute bridge vs hip thrust?
faq.a: The bridge starts from the floor with your back on the ground, while the hip thrust uses a bench and a longer range. The hip thrust is easier to load heavily.

faq.q: Do glute bridges build glutes?
faq.a: Yes, especially for beginners. Over time you will need to add load or single-leg work to keep progressing.

pike_push_up.summary: A push-up done with your hips raised into an inverted V, pressing your head toward the floor. It trains the shoulders vertically with bodyweight and builds toward handstand push-ups. Good for home training and calisthenics.
pike_push_up.musclesNote: The front delts and triceps press the body up, with the upper chest assisting. Raising the feet on a box makes it more vertical and shifts more work to the shoulders.
setup: Start in a push-up position, then walk your feet toward your hands and lift your hips.
Keep your hands about shoulder width apart.
Hold your head between your arms, looking back toward your feet.
Keep your legs fairly straight.
execution: Bend your elbows and lower the top of your head toward the floor in front of your hands.
Keep elbows at about 45 degrees from the body.
Press back up until the arms are straight.
Keep the hips high throughout.

mistakes.fix: Keep hips high so the body stays in an inverted V.
Keep the elbows angled back at about 45 degrees.
Lower your head forward of your hands so you form a triangle with your hands.

pike_push_up.progression: Build to 10-15 reps, then elevate your feet on a box. Next, progress toward wall handstand push-ups.

faq.q: Do pike push-ups build shoulders?
faq.a: Yes. They train the front delts and triceps with a vertical press. Raising the feet makes them harder.

faq.q: Pike push-ups vs handstand push-ups?
faq.a: Pike push-ups are easier and a common stepping stone. Handstand push-ups load your full bodyweight vertically.

reverse_fly_db.summary: A bent-over or chest-supported exercise where you raise dumbbells out to the sides. It targets the rear delts and helps balance pressing work. Good for most lifters looking to build shoulder balance and posture.
reverse_fly_db.musclesNote: The rear delts pull the arms out and back, with the rhomboids and mid traps assisting. Keeping the arms wider and slightly soft at the elbow keeps the focus on the rear delts.
setup: Hinge forward at the hips until your torso is near parallel, or lie chest-down on an incline bench.
Hold light dumbbells under your chest with palms facing each other.
Keep a slight bend in the elbows.
Brace your trunk and keep your neck neutral.
execution: Raise the dumbbells out to the sides in a wide arc.
Stop when your arms are about level with your torso.
Lower slowly for 2-3 seconds.
Lead with the elbows, not the hands.

mistakes.fix: Choose light dumbbells you can raise without swinging.
Focus on moving the arms out wide rather than pinching the blades together.
Keep your torso still or use a chest-supported bench.

reverse_fly_db.progression: Use higher reps, around 12-20, and add weight in small jumps. If dumbbell jumps are too big, add reps or a pause at the top.

faq.q: What do reverse flies work?
faq.a: Mainly the rear delts, with the rhomboids and mid traps assisting.

faq.q: Reverse fly vs face pull?
faq.a: Both train the rear delts. The reverse fly isolates them more, while the face pull adds rotator cuff work.

band_pull_apart.summary: A band exercise where you pull a band apart from arm's length to your chest. It trains the rear delts and upper back with almost no setup or recovery cost. Good as a warm-up before pressing or as high-rep accessory work for anyone.
band_pull_apart.musclesNote: The rear delts pull the arms horizontally backward, while the rhomboids and mid traps draw the shoulder blades together at the end. An overhand grip leans more on the rear delts; an underhand grip brings in a bit more of the mid back.
setup: Hold a light band with an overhand grip, hands about shoulder width apart.
Raise your arms straight in front of you to shoulder height.
Keep a slight bend in the elbows.
Stand tall with your ribs down and abs lightly braced.
execution: Pull the band apart by moving your hands out to the sides until it touches your chest.
Keep your arms at shoulder height as you pull.
Pause for a second with the shoulder blades squeezed together.
Return slowly, keeping tension on the band all the way back.

mistakes.fix: Keep the shoulders down away from the ears and use a lighter band if they creep up.

mistakes.mistake: Bending the elbows into a row
mistakes.fix: Keep the arms nearly straight so the rear delts move the load.
Brace your abs and keep your ribs stacked over your hips.

band_pull_apart.progression: Start with 15-25 reps per set. Progress with a narrower grip, a stronger band, a pause at the end, or more total reps across the week.

faq.q: Are band pull-aparts good for posture?
faq.a: They strengthen the rear delts and upper back, which helps balance a lot of pressing. They will not fix posture on their own, but they are a cheap way to keep the back of the shoulders in proportion.

faq.q: How often can you do band pull-aparts?
faq.a: Because the load is light and they cause little soreness, many lifters do a few sets most days or before every upper-body session. Cut back if your shoulders feel irritated.

calf_raise_bb.summary: A standing calf raise with a barbell across your upper back and the balls of the feet on a block. It lets you load the calves heavily without a dedicated calf machine. Good for lifters in gyms without a calf machine, as long as they can stay balanced.
calf_raise_bb.musclesNote: With straight knees the gastrocnemius does most of the work lifting the heel, with the soleus assisting. The trunk and upper back hold the bar steady, and balance is often the limiting factor.
setup: Set up in a squat rack with the safeties just below the bar's lowest point, or use a Smith machine.
Place the bar across your upper back as for a back squat.
Put the balls of your feet on a sturdy plate or low block, heels free.
Stand with knees straight but not locked and your trunk braced.
execution: Lower your heels until you feel a deep stretch in the calves.
Pause for about a second at the bottom.
Press through the balls of your feet, especially the big toe, to rise as high as you can.
Hold the top briefly, then lower for 2-3 seconds.

mistakes.fix: Pause in the stretch so the calves, not the Achilles' rebound, start each rep.
Use a block high enough to get a real stretch and rise all the way up each rep.
Train inside a rack with safeties set, or move to a Smith machine.

calf_raise_bb.progression: Add reps until you reach about 12-15 with full range, then add 10 lb. Calves tend to respond to pauses and slow lowering as much as to more weight.

faq.q: Are barbell calf raises effective?
faq.a: Yes. They let you load the calves heavily, which is otherwise hard without a machine. The main drawback is balance, so a Smith machine is a good substitute.

faq.q: How many sets should I do for calves?
faq.a: A common starting point is 3-4 hard sets, 2-3 times per week. Adjust based on how your calves recover and progress.

calf_raise_db.summary: A standing calf raise holding a dumbbell, most often done one leg at a time on a step. It is simple to set up and lets each calf work on its own. Good for home gyms, beginners, and anyone with one calf weaker than the other.
calf_raise_db.musclesNote: The gastrocnemius and soleus lift the heel, with the gastrocnemius doing more when the knee is straight. Going single-leg roughly doubles the load per calf without needing heavy dumbbells.
setup: Stand on a step with the ball of one foot on the edge and the heel hanging off.
Hold a dumbbell in the hand on the same side as the working leg.
Hold a rail or wall with your free hand for balance.
Keep the working knee straight and hook the other foot behind your ankle.
execution: Lower your heel slowly until you feel a full stretch.
Pause for about a second at the bottom.
Rise as high as you can onto the ball of your foot.
Squeeze at the top, then lower for 2-3 seconds.

mistakes.fix: Pause in the stretch to take momentum out of the rep.
Lower all the way into the stretch and rise all the way up each rep.

mistakes.mistake: Rolling to the outside of the foot
mistakes.fix: Keep pressure through the big toe as you rise.

calf_raise_db.progression: Push reps toward 15-20 before moving up a dumbbell size. Single-leg work is the main way to make dumbbell calf raises heavy enough for stronger lifters.

faq.q: Are single-leg calf raises better than double-leg?
faq.a: For dumbbell work, usually yes. You get more load per calf with light dumbbells, and each side has to work on its own.

faq.q: Do calf raises need a full range of motion?
faq.a: Yes. Getting a deep stretch at the bottom and a full rise at the top is more productive than short, bouncy reps.

calf_raise_bw.summary: A calf raise using only bodyweight, ideally on a step so the heels can drop below the toes. It is a good entry point for beginners, a warm-up for lower-body days, and a base for single-leg work. Anyone can do it anywhere.
calf_raise_bw.musclesNote: The gastrocnemius and soleus lift the heels; straight knees bias the gastrocnemius. For trained lifters, two-leg bodyweight raises are light, so single-leg reps are usually needed to make them challenging.
setup: Stand on a step with the balls of your feet on the edge and heels hanging off.
Hold a wall or rail lightly for balance.
Keep your knees straight but not locked.
execution: Lower your heels slowly until you feel a stretch in the calves.
Pause for a second at the bottom.
Rise up as high as you can onto the balls of your feet.
Hold the top briefly, then lower for 2-3 seconds.

mistakes.fix: Pause at the bottom of every rep so the muscles do the work.

mistakes.mistake: Doing it flat on the floor
mistakes.fix: Use a step so the heels can drop and you get a fuller range.
Use a slow lowering and a pause at the top.

calf_raise_bw.progression: Build to 20-30 slow reps, then switch to single-leg raises. Once those are easy for 15-20, add a dumbbell.

faq.q: Do bodyweight calf raises build muscle?
faq.a: They can for beginners, especially with full range and slow reps. Most people will need single-leg work or added weight to keep progressing.

faq.q: How many calf raises should I do?
faq.a: Start with 2-3 sets of 15-20 with full range. Add reps or move to single-leg once that feels easy.

close_grip_bench.summary: A barbell bench press with a grip about shoulder width, narrower than a standard bench. It shifts more of the work to the triceps while still allowing heavy loads. Good for lifters building triceps strength or improving their bench press lockout.
close_grip_bench.musclesNote: The triceps straighten the elbow and handle more of the work than in a regular bench, while the chest and front delts still contribute heavily. Elbows staying closer to the body increase the triceps' share.
setup: Lie on the bench with your eyes under the bar.
Grip the bar about shoulder width, with wrists stacked over the elbows.
Pull your shoulder blades back and down and keep a slight arch.
Plant your feet flat and unrack the bar to straight arms over your shoulders.
execution: Lower the bar to your lower chest with elbows tucked about 30-45 degrees from your sides.
Touch the chest lightly without bouncing.
Press the bar back up and slightly back toward your shoulders.
Lock out fully, keeping your wrists straight.

mistakes.fix: Use about shoulder width; a very narrow grip strains the wrists without extra benefit.
Keep the elbows tucked so the triceps do more work.
Control the descent and touch the chest lightly.

close_grip_bench.progression: Add 5 lb once you hit your target reps, usually 5-10 per set. When progress stalls, try paused reps or floor presses to keep building.

faq.q: Is close grip bench good for triceps?
faq.a: Yes. It is one of the best ways to load the triceps heavily. It also carries over well to the regular bench press.

faq.q: How close should the grip be on close grip bench?
faq.a: About shoulder width is usually best. Going narrower mostly adds wrist strain without adding triceps work.
